moments.title: Wundt opens the first psychology laboratory
moments.body:
Wundt establishes the first laboratory dedicated to experimental psychology in a former dining room. Students measure reaction times to flashing lights and ticking metronomes.

The goal is to separate psychology from philosophy by tying it to stopwatches, calibrated apparatus and trained observers.

quote.text: In psychology, the person looks upon himself as from within.

moments.takeaway: Psychology becomes an experimental discipline when measurement is added to introspection.

moments.title: Watson's behaviourist manifesto
moments.body:
Watson publishes 'Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It', insisting psychology study only observable behaviour.

The move sidelines introspection and unconscious explanation. American psychology will be dominated by behaviourism for the next four decades.
moments.takeaway: Demanding observability shaped what counted as data in the discipline for forty years.

moments.title: The cognitive revolution
moments.body:
At an MIT symposium and in linked publications, the assumption that minds can be modelled as information-processing systems takes hold.

Miller's 'magical number seven' (1956), Chomsky's 1959 review of Skinner, and Newell and Simon's Logic Theorist together reset the field.
moments.takeaway: Treating the mind as a computational system reopened questions behaviourism had closed.

now.title: Psychology today
now.body: Contemporary psychology spans cognitive neuroscience, computational modelling, large-scale replication efforts and clinical practice. The 2010s 'replication crisis' (Open Science Collaboration, 2015) has reshaped methodological standards.
now.open_questions: How robust are foundational findings under preregistration and adversarial collaboration? How should psychological evidence be weighted in policy?

items.reflection: Psychology's history shows recurring swings between observable behaviour and inferred mental processes. Each turn discards some claims and rescues others.

moments.title: Pavlov's digestion research begins
moments.body: Pavlov studies gastric secretion in dogs. His method, surgically isolating digestive juices, will win the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
moments.takeaway: Conditioning research begins as a by-product of physiology, not psychology.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: Pavlov is awarded the prize for digestive physiology, not psychology. The Conditional Reflex work follows over the next two decades.
moments.takeaway: Major figures are often recognised for one set of contributions and remembered for another.

moments.title: Conditioned Reflexes published in English
moments.body:
Anrep's English edition makes Pavlov's full account available to American psychologists, just as behaviourism is consolidating its dominance.

Watson had already invoked Pavlov in his 1913 manifesto.
moments.takeaway: Translation and publication timing shape which ideas reach which audiences.

now.title: Classical conditioning today
now.body: Conditioning paradigms remain central to learning theory, fear research and clinical exposure therapies. Computational models map the neural circuits involved (amygdala, prefrontal cortex).
now.open_questions: How do classical conditioning circuits interact with reinforcement learning models in machine learning?

items.reflection: Pavlov's work is often presented as the start of behaviourism. He himself was a physiologist who resisted that framing.

moments.title: Bowlby's 44 thieves
moments.body:
Bowlby publishes a study of 44 juvenile thieves and 44 controls, arguing maternal separation in early childhood predicts later antisocial behaviour.

The methods, with researcher-conducted interviews and a small sample, would not meet current standards.
moments.takeaway: Foundational studies can frame a field's questions while using methods later revised.

moments.title: Attachment and Loss volume one
moments.body:
Bowlby integrates ethology, evolutionary biology and clinical observation into a developmental theory of attachment.

The distinction between privation and deprivation will be sharpened by Michael Rutter (1981).
moments.takeaway: Cross-disciplinary integration produced a theory that outlived its original methods.

moments.title: Patterns of Attachment
moments.body:
Ainsworth's book details the Strange Situation procedure and the classifications: secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant.

Main and Solomon (1990) will later add disorganised attachment as a fourth category.
moments.takeaway: Operationalising a theory through a standardised procedure made empirical comparison possible.

now.title: Attachment research today
now.body: Cross-cultural research (van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg, 1988) showed proportions of attachment styles vary by culture. Meta-analyses link disorganised attachment with later mental health outcomes.
now.open_questions: How stable are early classifications into adulthood? How do interventions affect attachment outcomes for at-risk infants?

items.reflection: Bowlby developed his theory while working with children evacuated and bereaved during the Second World War. Historical context shapes which questions get asked.

moments.title: Eichmann on trial in Jerusalem
moments.body: The trial raises questions about how ordinary people participate in atrocity. Arendt later coins 'the banality of evil' (1963).
moments.takeaway: Postwar Europe shaped the questions academic psychology then took into the laboratory.

moments.title: Behavioral Study of Obedience
moments.body: Milgram reports that 26 of 40 participants delivered the maximum apparent shock under an experimenter's instruction. He frames the result as a finding about situational power, not personality.

quote.text: Stark authority was pitted against the subjects' strongest moral imperatives.

moments.takeaway: Situational pressure produced obedience far beyond expert and lay predictions.

moments.title: Burger's partial replication
moments.body:
Under modified ethical protocols, Burger obtains broadly similar obedience rates to a 150-volt cut-off point.

Later archival work (Perry, 2013) reopens questions about Milgram's data handling.
moments.takeaway: Even classic findings continue to be re-examined against new evidence.

now.title: Obedience research today
now.body: Modern variants use immersive virtual reality (Slater et al., 2006) to test responses without ethical violations. Meta-research focuses on individual differences and dissent dynamics.
now.open_questions: What conditions reliably increase resistance to harmful authority? How do online environments mediate similar dynamics?

items.reflection: Milgram's studies could not be run today. Their continued teaching depends on context about both their power and their costs.

moments.title: Syntactic Structures
moments.body:
Chomsky argues language could not be learned by reinforcement of word combinations because speakers produce sentences they have never heard.

He proposes generative grammar as a model of competence.
moments.takeaway: Productivity of language posed a problem behaviourist learning theory could not solve.

moments.title: Review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior
moments.body:
Chomsky's critique of Skinner's Verbal Behavior (1957) argues operant conditioning cannot account for syntactic productivity.

The review is widely credited with shifting the centre of psycholinguistics.
moments.takeaway: A single review can mark a generational turn in a discipline.

moments.title: Aspects of the Theory of Syntax
moments.body: Chomsky introduces the distinction between competence and performance and the idea of an innate Language Acquisition Device.
moments.takeaway: Nativist assumptions about language structure shaped cognitive science for decades.

now.title: Language and mind today
now.body: Large language models challenge some nativist claims about productivity. Statistical learning research (Saffran et al., 1996) shows infants extract structure from input. The debate over what is innate vs learned continues.
now.open_questions: What does the success of statistical language models say about innateness? How do bilingual brains organise multiple grammars?

items.reflection: Chomsky's critique demolished one paradigm but installed another whose own empirical commitments are now under review.

moments.title: Wundt opens the Leipzig laboratory
moments.body: Wundt establishes the first laboratory dedicated to experimental psychology in a former dining room at the University of Leipzig. He trains graduate students from across Europe and the US in calibrated apparatus, reaction-time measurement, and 'trained introspection' under controlled conditions.

quote.text: In psychology, the person looks upon himself as from within.

moments.takeaway: Psychology becomes a discipline distinct from philosophy at the moment it adopts the laboratory.

moments.title: The Wundt diaspora
moments.body: By 1900, Wundt had supervised around 180 doctoral dissertations. His students included G. Stanley Hall (founded the first US psychology laboratory at Johns Hopkins, 1883), Edward Titchener (Cornell, structuralism), Hugo Münsterberg, James McKeen Cattell.
moments.takeaway: A single laboratory's training shaped the formation of psychology departments across two continents in two decades.

now.title: Wundt's legacy
now.body: Reaction time methodology is foundational to modern cognitive psychology and cognitive neuroscience (e.g., Stroop task, lexical decision tasks). The introspective methods Wundt championed were sidelined by behaviourism but have returned in subjective reports paired with brain imaging.
now.open_questions: What is the role of first-person reports in a brain-based psychology? Phenomenology and consciousness studies are still finding their footing.

items.reflection: Most disciplines have founding myths. Psychology's founding moment is unusually well-documented and unusually instrumental — a single room, a single set of stopwatches, training a generation.

moments.title: James's Harvard laboratory
moments.body: James sets up a small laboratory at Harvard for psychological demonstrations — contested as either the first or among the earliest in the US. He is more philosopher than experimentalist by temperament.
moments.takeaway: American psychology begins as a hybrid of philosophy and physiology.

moments.title: The Principles of Psychology
moments.body: Twelve years in the writing, James's 'Principles' covers the stream of consciousness, habit, emotion (the James-Lange theory), self, will. The book defines what psychology can and should address. James himself disliked teaching it: 'A loathsome, distended, tumefied, bloated, dropsical mass.'

quote.text: Habit is thus the enormous fly-wheel of society, its most precious conservative agent.

moments.takeaway: American psychology's foundational textbook frames the subject for a generation.

now.title: Pragmatism today
now.body: James's pragmatism (1907) and emphasis on functional consequences of mental states resonates with modern cognitive science and ecological psychology. The stream of consciousness concept influenced literature (Joyce, Woolf) as much as psychology.
now.open_questions: What is consciousness 'for' functionally? The hard problem James named is still open.

items.reflection: James was sceptical of his own discipline's overreach. His acknowledgment that psychology might never become a strict science remains a useful corrective to disciplinary overconfidence.

moments.title: The Interpretation of Dreams
moments.body: Freud publishes 'Die Traumdeutung' (dated 1900 but printed November 1899). The book argues that dreams are wish-fulfilments expressing unconscious desires, accessible through symbolic interpretation. Sales were initially poor (600 copies in eight years) but the book founded psychoanalysis as a movement.
moments.takeaway: A book that didn't sell became one of the most influential works of the 20th century.

moments.title: Clark University lectures
moments.who: Freud, Jung, Ferenczi visit the US
moments.body: Freud delivers five lectures at Clark University in Worcester, Massachusetts, at the invitation of G. Stanley Hall. The lectures introduce psychoanalysis to a major American audience.
moments.takeaway: American psychology absorbed Freud's ideas selectively; psychoanalysis became influential in psychiatry and culture more than in academic psychology.

now.title: Freud after Freud
now.body: Academic psychology has largely moved beyond Freud's specific theories, which were not testable in the modern sense. His broader claims — that much of mental life is not consciously accessible, that early experience shapes adult psychology, that defense mechanisms operate — have found partial support in cognitive psychology, attachment research, and trauma studies. The clinical influence remains substantial in psychodynamic therapy.
now.open_questions: How much of Freud's insight survives empirical examination? The answer is 'less than he claimed but more than zero'.

items.reflection: Freud is the rare figure whose work shaped 20th-century literature, art and politics as much as his discipline. Academic psychology's relationship with his legacy is uneasy: dismissed as unfalsifiable, kept as a historical reference, reread occasionally as cognitive science rediscovers unconscious processing.

moments.title: The Behavior of Organisms
moments.body: Skinner publishes 'The Behavior of Organisms', detailing operant conditioning. The 'operant chamber' (popularly the Skinner box) allows precise measurement of how reinforcement schedules shape behaviour. Schedules of reinforcement (fixed-ratio, variable-ratio, fixed-interval, variable-interval) produce reliable patterns.
moments.takeaway: Behaviour can be shaped by environmental contingencies — and measured to a precision other branches of psychology envied.

moments.title: Walden Two to Beyond Freedom and Dignity
moments.body: Skinner extends his vision to social organisation. Walden Two (1948) imagines a behaviourist utopia. Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971) argues 'autonomous man' is an unhelpful fiction. The book attracts both intense interest and intense criticism.
moments.takeaway: Behavioural science as a vision for social engineering — controversial then, with echoes now in 'nudge' and behavioural design.

now.title: Operant conditioning today
now.body: Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) is used in education and clinical settings (notably autism intervention, where it is also controversial). Variable-ratio reinforcement schedules underpin slot machines and many engagement features of social media platforms. The basic principles remain robust; the ethical applications continue to be debated.
now.open_questions: What is the boundary between using behavioural principles for the user's benefit and for an institution's?

items.reflection: Skinner's empirical work was meticulous; his philosophical extension was sweeping. Both have outlasted the strict behaviourism of his time.

moments.title: Forty-Four Juvenile Thieves
moments.who: John Bowlby, London Child Guidance Clinic
moments.body: Bowlby's study of 44 juvenile thieves and 44 controls argues that 'affectionless psychopathy' correlates with maternal separation in early childhood. The study has methodological limitations (interviews conducted by the clinician), but the framing question — does early relational disruption shape later behaviour? — sets a research agenda.
moments.takeaway: Clinical observation generates the hypothesis that decades of subsequent work refine.

moments.title: Maternal Care and Mental Health
moments.body: Bowlby's WHO report on the mental health of homeless children synthesises wartime evidence on orphans and evacuees. It argues for the importance of continuous early care. The report shaped postwar attitudes to maternal employment and institutional care in ways that exceeded the evidence.
moments.takeaway: Policy uptake of psychological research can outrun what the research strictly supports.

moments.title: Attachment and Loss trilogy
moments.body: Bowlby integrates ethology (Lorenz's imprinting work), evolutionary biology and clinical observation into Attachment (1969), Separation (1973) and Loss (1980). The theoretical framework is mature when Mary Ainsworth (his collaborator from the 1950s) operationalises it through the Strange Situation.
moments.takeaway: A theory that drew on a wider intellectual base than typical mid-century psychology proved more durable.

now.title: Attachment today
now.body: Attachment theory has been extended to adult romantic relationships (Hazan & Shaver, 1987), to clinical practice (Attachment-Based Family Therapy), and to neuroscience of social bonding. Cross-cultural research has refined the original claims; the broad framework remains influential.
now.open_questions: How modifiable are attachment patterns through intervention? Some evidence for plasticity into adulthood; the specific routes remain studied.

items.reflection: Bowlby worked through the Second World War's mass displacement of children. The historical context shaped which questions felt urgent — and shaped policy responses that the theory itself didn't strictly entail.

moments.title: Cognitive revolution year
moments.body: Several pivotal events in one year: George Miller's 'Magical Number Seven' paper (March); Allen Newell and Herbert Simon demonstrate Logic Theorist at the Dartmouth AI Workshop (summer); Noam Chomsky presents 'Three Models of Language' at MIT's Symposium on Information Theory (September); Bruner, Goodnow & Austin publish 'A Study of Thinking'.
moments.takeaway: A cluster of independent developments crystallised the information-processing approach to mind.

moments.title: Chomsky's review of Skinner
moments.body: Chomsky's devastating review of Skinner's 'Verbal Behavior' (Language, 1959) argues that productivity of language cannot be explained by operant conditioning. The review marks the moment behaviourism's claim to explain everything becomes untenable.
moments.takeaway: A single 31-page review changed the centre of gravity of an entire discipline.

moments.title: Cognitive Psychology textbook
moments.body: Neisser's textbook 'Cognitive Psychology' gives the field a name and consolidates the new approach. The information-processing metaphor — mind as computer — becomes dominant.
moments.takeaway: A textbook canonises what had been a loose collection of researchers.

now.title: Cognitive science today
now.body: The information-processing approach gave way to embodied, embedded, situated cognition in some quarters; rejoined neuroscience in others (cognitive neuroscience from the 1990s). Modern cognitive science includes computational modelling, fMRI, behavioural experiments and philosophy of mind. Large language models have revived debates Chomsky's review seemed to settle.
now.open_questions: What does the success of statistical language models tell us about the structure of human language and cognition?

items.reflection: Paradigm shifts in psychology often look in retrospect like a single year. Up close, they were the consolidation of work done over decades by people who weren't sure where it was going.

moments.title: DSM-I published
moments.body: The first Diagnostic and Statistical Manual covers 106 disorders, heavily influenced by psychoanalytic concepts. Homosexuality is listed as a sociopathic personality disturbance.
moments.takeaway: Psychiatric classification began as a frame that reflected its era's assumptions.

moments.title: Homosexuality declassified
moments.who: APA board, after activist pressure and the Rosenhan experiment
moments.body: After campaigns by gay rights activists and increasing professional doubt, the APA removes homosexuality from DSM-II. Robert Spitzer's role in driving the change was central. David Rosenhan's 'On Being Sane in Insane Places' (Science, 1973) had highlighted diagnostic unreliability.
moments.takeaway: Diagnostic categories can be revised as social attitudes and evidence shift.

moments.title: DSM-III shifts to operationalised criteria
moments.body: DSM-III moves to explicit diagnostic criteria for each disorder, modelling reliability rather than aetiology. The descriptive approach replaces the psychodynamic framing. PTSD enters the manual.
moments.takeaway: Reliability improves at the cost of theoretical depth — a deliberate trade-off.

moments.title: DSM-5 maintains the categorical framework
moments.body: DSM-5 makes incremental changes (autism spectrum, gender dysphoria, removal of grief exclusion for major depression) but preserves the categorical structure. NIMH's RDoC initiative (announced 2013) signals a research push toward dimensional alternatives.
moments.takeaway: Operational structure has been remarkably stable; clinical realities and research evidence have changed around it.

now.title: Classification today
now.body: ICD-11 (WHO, 2022) includes some dimensional elements (especially for personality disorders). HiTOP (Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology, 2017) offers a structured dimensional alternative. Categorical diagnosis persists because insurance, research and clinical communication require labels.
now.open_questions: Can dimensional and categorical approaches coexist clinically? Most modern frameworks try to hybrid.

items.reflection: Classification systems carry the assumptions of their era. The history of the DSM is partly a history of what each generation considered worth pathologising.

moments.title: Beck develops cognitive therapy
moments.who: Aaron T. Beck, University of Pennsylvania
moments.body: Beck, trained as a psychoanalyst, notices that depressed patients have automatic negative thoughts about themselves, the world and the future ('cognitive triad'). He develops cognitive therapy, focusing on identifying and challenging these thoughts. Albert Ellis had developed Rational Emotive Therapy in parallel from 1955.
moments.takeaway: Clinical observation by a working psychoanalyst yields a new therapy.

moments.title: Cognitive Therapy of Depression
moments.body: The book sets out cognitive therapy for depression as a structured, short-term, manualised approach. Randomised trials in the 1970s-80s show comparable efficacy to antidepressants for many patients.
moments.takeaway: Cognitive therapy becomes one of the first psychotherapies with structured efficacy evidence.

moments.title: Cognitive-behavioural integration
moments.who: Beck and others integrate with behavioural therapy
moments.body: Combined cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) integrates Beck's cognitive techniques with behavioural activation, exposure and skills training. It becomes the dominant evidence-based psychotherapy through the 1990s.
moments.takeaway: Integration of complementary techniques produces a more flexible therapeutic approach.

now.title: CBT today
now.body: CBT is the most-researched psychotherapy; NICE guidelines recommend it for many conditions. UK's IAPT programme (2008) made CBT widely available. Third-wave variants (DBT for borderline personality, ACT for chronic conditions, mindfulness-based approaches) extend the framework. Routine outcomes data show effectiveness in real-world conditions, though smaller than RCT effects.
now.open_questions: Is CBT effective because of its specific techniques or because of common therapy factors (alliance, hope)? Dismantling studies have produced mixed answers.

items.reflection: Beck died in 2021 aged 100, having seen his clinical innovation become one of the most-used psychotherapies in the world. The arc from observation to manualised treatment to evidence-based default took 60 years.

moments.title: Bem's precognition paper triggers methodological scrutiny
moments.body: Bem publishes 'Feeling the Future' in JPSP, claiming evidence for precognition — extra-sensory perception of future events. The paper used standard psychology methods. Critics including Wagenmakers argued the methods themselves were the problem; if standard practices could produce 'evidence' for the impossible, what did that say about other 'significant' findings?
moments.takeaway: An extraordinary claim made with ordinary methods exposed the ordinariness of the problem.

moments.title: Reproducibility Project: Psychology
moments.who: Open Science Collaboration, led by Brian Nosek
moments.body: 270 researchers attempted to replicate 100 published psychology findings. 36% replicated; effect sizes were on average about half the originals. The Science paper became one of the most-cited psychology papers of the decade.
moments.takeaway: A coordinated test of the field's published findings produced uncomfortable but actionable results.

moments.title: Methodological reform
moments.body: Preregistration, registered reports, the OSF (Open Science Framework, 2013), badges for open data, the TOP guidelines (2014). Many landmark findings — ego depletion, power posing, the marshmallow test as a predictor of life outcomes — have been substantially revised or weakened on replication.
moments.takeaway: The reforms haven't fully fixed the field but have changed publishing norms across leading psychology journals.

now.title: Open science today
now.body: Preregistration is increasingly default for confirmatory studies. Registered reports appear in over 300 journals. Massive collaborations (the Many Labs projects, Psychological Science Accelerator) enable replication at scale. Adversarial collaborations (e.g., Kahneman-style) test specific claims with both sides' methods. The crisis has spread beyond psychology to medicine, economics and machine learning.
now.open_questions: How robust are findings being produced now? The reforms are improving quality but the pipeline is long; full effects on published literature will take decades.

items.reflection: The replication crisis is a story of a discipline correcting itself, painfully and incompletely. Other fields are at earlier stages of the same realisation.

moments.title: Principles of Psychology
moments.body:
James publishes the two-volume Principles of Psychology after twelve years of writing.

He coins 'stream of consciousness' and treats habit, emotion and self as functional adaptations.

quote.text: Consciousness, then, does not appear to itself chopped up in bits... it flows.

moments.takeaway: American functionalism asks what mental processes do, not just what they are.

moments.title: Briefer Course textbook
moments.body: James condenses the Principles into a teaching text known as 'Jimmy', while the original is 'James'.
moments.takeaway: Textbook decisions can outweigh original treatises in shaping a discipline's training.

moments.title: Pragmatism lectures
moments.body: James delivers public lectures on pragmatism, arguing truth is what proves useful in inquiry.
moments.takeaway: Pragmatist epistemology privileges what an idea does over what it asserts.

now.title: Functionalism's legacy
now.body: Evolutionary psychology, embodied cognition and ecological psychology carry James's question forward.
now.open_questions: Can functional explanations avoid the just-so storytelling critics charge against evolutionary psychology?

items.reflection: James trained as a doctor and taught physiology before psychology.

moments.title: The Interpretation of Dreams
moments.body: Freud's book, published November 1899 but dated 1900, proposes dreams as disguised wish-fulfilments and introduces the dynamic unconscious.

quote.text: The interpretation of dreams is the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious activities of the mind.

moments.takeaway: Freud's clinical method treats dreams as decodable texts about the unconscious.

moments.title: Three Essays on Sexuality
moments.body: Freud's account of infantile sexuality provokes outrage and consolidates the psychoanalytic movement.
moments.takeaway: Provocation and theoretical extension often arrive together.

moments.title: The Ego and the Id
moments.body: Freud introduces the structural model of id, ego and superego, replacing the earlier topographic model.
moments.takeaway: Even foundational theorists revise their own systems substantially.

now.title: Freud's contested legacy
now.body: Most empirical psychology treats Freud as historical. Neuropsychoanalysis revives some testable claims; cultural studies retain his framework.
now.open_questions: Which Freudian claims survive when reformulated in neuroscientific terms?

items.reflection: Freud's reach into 20th-century culture was vastly greater than his standing in academic psychology.

moments.title: Psychology as the Behaviourist Views It
moments.body: Watson's Psychological Review paper sets behaviourism's agenda: study only behaviour, abandon introspection.

quote.text: Give me a dozen healthy infants... and I'll guarantee to take any one at random and train him to become any type of specialist I might select.

moments.takeaway: A manifesto can redirect a field for decades.

moments.title: The Little Albert experiment
moments.body: Watson and Rayner condition an 11-month-old infant to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise. Ethics and methodology are disputed.
moments.takeaway: Iconic studies often turn out to be methodologically thinner than textbook accounts.

moments.title: Behaviourism revised edition
moments.body: Forced from academia after a scandal, Watson works in advertising, carrying behaviourist methods into consumer research.
moments.takeaway: Behaviourism shaped advertising as much as psychology.

now.title: Behaviourism's afterlife
now.body: Applied behaviour analysis, CBT and reinforcement learning in AI all carry behaviourist methods forward.
now.open_questions: Where do behaviourist explanations remain sufficient, and where are cognitive constructs unavoidable?

items.reflection: Watson's confidence about the malleability of behaviour set the tone for an era.

moments.title: The Behaviour of Organisms
moments.body: Skinner formalises operant conditioning, introducing the operant chamber and rate of response as the dependent variable.
moments.takeaway: A standardised apparatus lets a research programme accumulate comparable data.

moments.title: Verbal Behaviour
moments.body: Skinner extends operant principles to language. Chomsky's 1959 review will demolish the account.
moments.takeaway: Programmes overreach into adjacent territory at their own risk.

moments.title: Beyond Freedom and Dignity
moments.body: Skinner's popular book argues autonomous selfhood obstructs effective behaviour design. Time magazine cover and intense backlash.
moments.takeaway: Behaviourism's philosophical implications became as controversial as its methods.

now.title: Operant conditioning today
now.body: Behaviour analysis dominates evidence-based autism intervention. Reinforcement schedules underlie social media and game design.
now.open_questions: What ethical limits should constrain reinforcement-based design in apps for children?

items.reflection: Skinner thought he was building a science of behaviour; his readers focused on the philosophy.

moments.title: Uber das Gedachtnis
moments.body: Ebbinghaus uses himself as sole subject, learning 2,300 nonsense syllables. He plots the first quantitative forgetting curve and discovers the spacing effect.
moments.takeaway: Treating a phenomenon experimentally requires inventing materials that strip out confounds.

moments.title: English translation
moments.body: Memory is translated, making Ebbinghaus accessible to American verbal-learning researchers.
moments.takeaway: Translation timing shapes which experimental traditions dominate.

moments.title: Replication of the forgetting curve
moments.body: Murre and Dros replicate Ebbinghaus's curve in modern conditions, confirming its shape.
moments.takeaway: Classic findings can survive direct replication 130 years on.

now.title: Spacing in learning today
now.body: Spaced retrieval underlies tools from Anki to medical revision platforms. Spacing is among the most robust findings in cognitive psychology.
now.open_questions: Why is spacing so under-used in mainstream schooling despite the evidence?

items.reflection: Ebbinghaus self-experimented for years to produce a result that could fit on a single chart.

moments.title: Remembering
moments.body: Bartlett uses the Native American folktale 'War of the Ghosts' in serial reproduction. Participants distort the story in culturally systematic ways.
moments.takeaway: Memory is reconstructive, not reproductive.

moments.title: Bransford and Johnson context studies
moments.body: Comprehension and recall depend on having an appropriate schema at encoding.
moments.takeaway: Without a schema, even simple text is hard to remember.

moments.title: Brewer and Treyens office study
moments.body: Participants in a waiting room later 'recall' schema-consistent items (books) that were not present.
moments.takeaway: Schemas insert content as well as distort it.

now.title: Schema theory and eyewitness memory
now.body: Schema-driven distortions are central to modern accounts of eyewitness error and false memory.
now.open_questions: How can interview protocols minimise schema-driven distortion in legal contexts?

items.reflection: Bartlett's social-anthropological framing was ignored under behaviourism, then rediscovered.

moments.title: Human Memory: A Proposed System
moments.who: Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin, Stanford
moments.body: Atkinson and Shiffrin formalise the multi-store model: sensory register, STS, LTS with rehearsal-based transfer.
moments.takeaway: Boxes-and-arrows became the visual grammar of cognitive psychology.

moments.title: Glanzer and Cunitz serial position
moments.body: Free recall shows primacy and recency; delay removes recency but not primacy, supporting two stores.
moments.takeaway: Behavioural dissociations support architectural distinctions in memory.

moments.title: Patient HM described
moments.body: Henry Molaison's bilateral medial temporal lobectomy leaves short-term but not new long-term declarative memory.
moments.takeaway: A single patient can constrain a whole theoretical framework.

now.title: Beyond the multi-store model
now.body: Working memory replaced unitary STM. LTM is subdivided into episodic, semantic and procedural systems.
now.open_questions: How modular is memory really?

items.reflection: The Atkinson-Shiffrin diagram is still drawn in textbooks because it is teachable, not because it is current.

moments.title: Working memory model
moments.body: Baddeley and Hitch replace STM with a system of central executive, phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad.
moments.takeaway: A unitary short-term store cannot explain dual-task patterns.

moments.title: Episodic buffer added
moments.body: Baddeley adds the episodic buffer to bind information across modalities and link to long-term memory.
moments.takeaway: Models grow components as new findings demand.

moments.title: Word-length effect
moments.body: Span is set by how many items can be spoken in about two seconds, supporting a time-limited phonological loop.
moments.takeaway: Articulatory mechanisms set verbal short-term memory limits.

now.title: Working memory and education
now.body: Capacity predicts reading and maths attainment. Cognitive load theory in instruction is built on the model.
now.open_questions: Can working memory be trained? Transfer is limited and contested.

items.reflection: The model has remained dominant for fifty years because it generates testable predictions.

moments.title: Reconstruction of Automobile Destruction
moments.body: Loftus and Palmer show the verb ('smashed' vs 'hit') shifts speed estimates and later memory for broken glass.

quote.text: About how fast were the cars going when they smashed into each other?

moments.takeaway: A single word can reshape what witnesses report.

moments.title: Lost in the mall study
moments.body: Researchers implant a false memory of being lost in a mall in around a quarter of participants.
moments.takeaway: Whole episodes can be confabulated under suggestion.

moments.title: Repressed memory critique
moments.body: Loftus becomes a central critic of repressed-memory therapy and testifies in the 'memory wars'.
moments.takeaway: Cognitive psychology directly intersects with legal practice.

now.title: Eyewitness reform
now.body: Sequential lineups and double-blind administration are now standard in many jurisdictions, traceable to Loftus and colleagues.
now.open_questions: How should courts handle expert testimony on memory reliability?

items.reflection: Loftus's career shows how laboratory work can reshape evidentiary standards in real trials.

moments.title: The Nature of Love
moments.body: Harlow's APA presidential address shows infant rhesus monkeys clinging to cloth surrogates rather than wire feeders.

quote.text: Man cannot live by milk alone.

moments.takeaway: Attachment is not reducible to feeding.

moments.title: Total isolation studies
moments.body: Isolated monkeys show severe social and emotional pathology, recovering only partially with peer 'monkey therapists'.
moments.takeaway: Early social experience has enduring developmental effects.

moments.title: Ethical reckoning
moments.body: Critics including Peter Singer cite Harlow's 'pit of despair' studies in the emerging animal-rights movement.
moments.takeaway: Foundational findings sit alongside foundational ethical concerns.

now.title: Contact comfort revisited
now.body: Skin-to-skin and kangaroo care for premature infants are mainstream paediatric practice.
now.open_questions: How do digital substitutes for caregiver interaction affect infant attachment?

items.reflection: Harlow's work is taught both as landmark research and as a case study in research ethics.

moments.title: Ganda fieldwork
moments.body: Ainsworth's naturalistic observations of mother-infant pairs identify patterns later formalised as attachment styles.
moments.takeaway: Cross-cultural fieldwork preceded the laboratory procedure.

moments.title: Strange Situation procedure
moments.body: Ainsworth and Wittig publish the eight-episode procedure for assessing infant-caregiver attachment.
moments.takeaway: Operational procedures enable cumulative research.

moments.title: Disorganised attachment added
moments.body: A fourth category is identified, associated with frightening caregiver behaviour and later psychopathology.
moments.takeaway: Typologies are extended as edge cases accumulate.

now.title: Attachment across the lifespan
now.body: Adult attachment interviews link infant patterns to adult relationships. Cross-cultural distributions vary; classifications hold.
now.open_questions: How stable are attachment classifications across childhood, and what changes them?

items.reflection: Ainsworth's careful ethological observation gave attachment theory its empirical legs.

moments.title: Asch conformity experiments
moments.body: Participants matching line lengths conform to a unanimous wrong majority on about a third of critical trials.
moments.takeaway: Even unambiguous perceptual judgements yield to group pressure.

moments.title: Opinions and Social Pressure
moments.body: Asch publishes findings in Scientific American, bringing conformity research to a post-war public.
moments.takeaway: Cold War anxieties shaped which findings reached public attention.

moments.title: Bond and Smith meta-analysis
moments.body: A meta-analysis of 133 Asch-paradigm studies finds conformity rates declined and vary by individualism-collectivism.
moments.takeaway: Cultural and historical context shapes a foundational effect.

now.title: Conformity in the digital age
now.body: Online conformity, echo chambers and 'like' counts have revived the Asch paradigm with new cues.
now.open_questions: Do anonymous online contexts amplify or weaken majority influence?

items.reflection: Asch designed an unambiguous task to show that even unambiguous truth bends under social pressure.

moments.title: Stanford Prison Experiment
moments.body: Zimbardo's mock prison is halted after six days due to brutal behaviour from 'guards'. Zimbardo himself acted as superintendent.
moments.takeaway: Situational forces can rapidly shape role behaviour.

moments.title: BBC Prison Study
moments.body: A partial replication finds participants do not automatically adopt brutal guard roles.
moments.takeaway: Replications can recontextualise canonical findings.

moments.title: Archive reanalysis
moments.body: Investigations of original tapes show Zimbardo coached guards toward harshness, undermining textbook accounts.
moments.takeaway: Iconic studies sometimes look different when the archive is reopened.

now.title: Identity and situation
now.body: Modern social identity approaches emphasise active identification with roles rather than mechanical role-taking.
now.open_questions: How should ethics committees evaluate prospective research with similar risks today?

items.reflection: Stanford Prison is taught as much for its ethical failings as for its findings.

moments.title: Minimal group experiments
moments.body: Tajfel finds arbitrary group assignment (Klee vs Kandinsky preference) produces in-group favouritism in resource allocation.
moments.takeaway: Mere categorisation suffices for discrimination.

moments.title: Social Identity Theory
moments.body: Tajfel and Turner integrate findings into a theory linking self-concept, group membership and intergroup behaviour.
moments.takeaway: A theory linking personal and social identity reframed prejudice research.

moments.title: Self-Categorization Theory
moments.body: Turner argues situational salience shifts whether people behave as individuals or group members.
moments.takeaway: Identity is dynamic, not fixed.

now.title: Social identity in politics
now.body: Brexit, populism and partisan polarisation are widely analysed through Tajfel's framework.
now.open_questions: How do online platforms construct and amplify identity-based mobilisation?

items.reflection: Tajfel, a Holocaust survivor, set out to understand how ordinary categorisation could become catastrophic.

moments.title: Robbers Cave experiment
moments.body: Two groups of 11-year-old boys at summer camp are divided, then put into competition, then required to cooperate on superordinate goals.
moments.takeaway: Cooperation requires shared goals no group can reach alone.

moments.title: Intergroup Conflict and Cooperation
moments.body: The full monograph is published, framing realistic conflict theory.
moments.takeaway: Group conflict has structural causes, not just psychological ones.

moments.title: Reanalysis by Gina Perry
moments.body: Perry's archival research reveals an earlier, abandoned Sherif study and more researcher intervention than reported.
moments.takeaway: Field experiments leave archives later researchers can reopen.

now.title: Realistic conflict in policy
now.body: Refugee integration, school desegregation and diversity programmes draw on superordinate-goal logic.
now.open_questions: What counts as a superordinate goal in deeply polarised contexts?

items.reflection: Sherif left Turkey under political pressure; his research carries the imprint of intergroup violence.

moments.title: Cognitive Maps in Rats and Men
moments.body: Tolman argues rats build cognitive maps of mazes rather than S-R chains.
moments.takeaway: Behaviour can be purposive and representational even in rats.

moments.title: Latent learning study
moments.body: Rats that explored a maze without reward later learn faster than naive rats, suggesting silent learning.
moments.takeaway: Learning is not strictly tied to immediate reinforcement.

moments.title: Nobel Prize for place and grid cells
moments.body: The Nobel recognises hippocampal place cells and entorhinal grid cells, the neural substrate of cognitive maps.
moments.takeaway: Behavioural concepts of representation can find a neural home decades later.

now.title: Cognitive maps in neuroscience
now.body: Place and grid cell research links spatial navigation to memory and decision-making more generally.
now.open_questions: How general is the cognitive-map framework beyond physical navigation?

items.reflection: Tolman wrote inside behaviourism and against it at the same time.

moments.title: The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two
moments.body: Miller's paper synthesises decades of data on absolute judgement and immediate memory, proposing a capacity limit around seven items.

quote.text: My problem is that I have been persecuted by an integer.

moments.takeaway: Disparate experimental traditions converge on a common capacity limit.

moments.title: Plans and the Structure of Behaviour
moments.body: TOTE units (test-operate-test-exit), an early information-processing model of action.
moments.takeaway: Cybernetic ideas re-entered psychology through the cognitive revolution.

moments.title: Cowan's magical number four
moments.body: Cowan argues the true capacity, when controlling for chunking and rehearsal, is closer to four.
moments.takeaway: Even foundational numbers get revised by tighter methodology.

now.title: Capacity limits in instructional design
now.body: Cognitive load theory, multimedia learning principles and UX design all reference working memory limits.
now.open_questions: How does individual variation in capacity affect equity in instructional design?

items.reflection: Miller's paper is famous partly for its style; he opens with persecution by a number.

moments.title: Syntactic Structures
moments.body: Chomsky's short monograph proposes generative grammar and transforms linguistics.
moments.takeaway: A formal apparatus reframed how language was studied.

moments.title: Review of Verbal Behaviour
moments.body: Chomsky's review of Skinner argues operant principles cannot explain creative language use.

quote.text: When we ask seriously to what extent terms such as 'stimulus' apply, we find this domain greatly restricted.

moments.takeaway: Decisive critique can shift a field even without an alternative empirical programme.

moments.title: Aspects of the Theory of Syntax
moments.body: Chomsky introduces the language acquisition device and the competence-performance distinction.
moments.takeaway: Nativist accounts return to centre stage in psychology of language.

now.title: Language acquisition debate
now.body: Usage-based accounts (Tomasello, Saffran) challenge strong nativism; large language models reopen questions about poverty of the stimulus.
now.open_questions: What do LLMs tell us, if anything, about human language acquisition?

items.reflection: Chomsky shaped half a century of linguistics from a single MIT corridor.

moments.title: Judgement under uncertainty
moments.body: Their Science paper catalogues representativeness, availability and anchoring as systematic shortcuts in judgement.
moments.takeaway: Errors are systematic, not random; cognition can be studied through its mistakes.

moments.title: Prospect Theory
moments.body: Their Econometrica paper proposes a descriptive theory of choice under risk, with loss aversion and probability weighting.
moments.takeaway: Descriptive and normative theories of choice diverge measurably.

moments.title: Nobel Prize in Economics
moments.body: Kahneman receives the Nobel for prospect theory (Tversky had died in 1996).
moments.takeaway: Psychological research can reshape another discipline's foundations.

now.title: Behavioural science in policy
now.body: Behavioural insights teams operate in many governments; defaults in pensions, organ donation and tax compliance reflect heuristics-and-biases findings.
now.open_questions: Which biases replicate robustly, and which were inflated by the original literature?

items.reflection: Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011) brought decades of work to a mass audience.

moments.title: Phineas Gage's accident
moments.body: A tamping iron is driven through railway foreman Phineas Gage's head. He survives, but his personality reportedly changes.
moments.takeaway: A single case can suggest brain localisation of personality.

moments.title: Recovery and Relapse paper
moments.body: Harlow's belated report describes Gage as 'no longer Gage'; later evidence suggests reports exaggerated the changes.
moments.takeaway: The historical record of single cases is often unreliable.

moments.title: Damasio's reconstruction
moments.body: The Damasios use Gage's skull to reconstruct the lesion, locating it in ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
moments.takeaway: Modern imaging can reanalyse historical cases.

now.title: Prefrontal cortex and decision-making
now.body: Ventromedial prefrontal lesions impair real-life decision-making despite intact intelligence (Bechara's Iowa Gambling Task).
now.open_questions: How do affective and cognitive contributions to decision-making interact in the prefrontal cortex?

items.reflection: Gage is a teaching staple because his story is dramatic, even where the evidence is thin.

moments.title: First split-brain patient
moments.body: Surgical sectioning of the corpus callosum to treat epilepsy yields patients in whom hemispheres can be tested independently.
moments.takeaway: Clinical surgery creates a natural experiment in lateralisation.

moments.title: Hemispheric specialisation studies
moments.body: Tachistoscope studies reveal each hemisphere has distinct capacities for language, spatial processing and emotion.
moments.takeaway: Lateralisation can be tested with controlled presentation.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: Sperry shares the Nobel Prize in Physiology with Hubel and Wiesel.
moments.takeaway: Split-brain work was recognised at the highest level.

now.title: Beyond simple lateralisation
now.body: Popular 'left brain / right brain' narratives oversimplify findings. Network neuroscience emphasises distributed processing.
now.open_questions: How do consciousness and unified selfhood emerge from coordinated hemispheric processing?

items.reflection: Split-brain research is taught both for what it shows about the brain and for the philosophical questions it opens about selfhood.

moments.title: Bilateral medial temporal lobectomy
moments.body: Scoville removes Henry Molaison's hippocampus to treat epilepsy. Severe anterograde amnesia results.
moments.takeaway: Surgical intervention can produce unintended cognitive losses.

moments.title: Scoville and Milner case report
moments.body: Their report establishes the hippocampus as essential for forming new declarative long-term memories.
moments.takeaway: A single case can found a major area of cognitive neuroscience.

moments.title: HM's death and brain donation
moments.who: Suzanne Corkin and the Brain Observatory
moments.body: Molaison's brain is sliced into 2,401 sections and made publicly available for research.
moments.takeaway: Long-term participation in research can extend beyond death.

now.title: Memory systems mapped
now.body: Multiple memory systems (episodic, semantic, procedural, working) are well-established with distinct substrates.
now.open_questions: How do hippocampal and neocortical contributions interact in long-term consolidation?

items.reflection: HM's case shaped 50 years of memory research while he remained anonymous to all but his researchers.

moments.title: Genie discovered
moments.body: A 13-year-old girl raised in extreme isolation is discovered with minimal language.
moments.takeaway: Tragic natural experiments raise questions about critical periods.

moments.title: Curtiss case study
moments.body: Curtiss documents Genie's language development; she acquires vocabulary but not full syntax.
moments.takeaway: Critical-period hypotheses receive partial support, with caveats.

moments.title: Research funding ended
moments.body: Disputes and ethics concerns end systematic study; Genie returns to foster care.
moments.takeaway: Long-term case-study research depends on arrangements that may collapse.

now.title: Critical periods refined
now.body: Sensitive periods are now seen as gradients, with second-language acquisition showing partial recovery.
now.open_questions: How much can early experience be compensated for by later intervention?

items.reflection: Genie's case sits uncomfortably between scientific opportunity and human responsibility.

moments.title: Depression: Clinical, Experimental, Theoretical Aspects
moments.body: Beck reframes depression as driven by negative thoughts about self, world and future, the cognitive triad.
moments.takeaway: Reformulating a disorder cognitively opens a new treatment target.

moments.title: Cognitive Therapy and the Emotional Disorders
moments.body: Beck systematises cognitive therapy techniques, including thought records and behavioural experiments.
moments.takeaway: Treatment manuals enable training and replication.

moments.title: Cognitive Therapy of Depression
moments.body: The clinical manual establishes CBT as a measurable, manualised treatment ready for randomised trials.
moments.takeaway: Manualisation made CBT competitive in evidence-based practice.

now.title: CBT mainstreamed
now.body: CBT is recommended in NICE guidelines for depression, anxiety and PTSD. Digital CBT and third-wave variants extend the field.
now.open_questions: Why have CBT outcomes plateaued in recent meta-analyses?

items.reflection: Beck, trained as a psychoanalyst, came to cognitive therapy through failed experiments designed to support analytic theory.

moments.title: Rational Therapy
moments.body: Ellis breaks with psychoanalysis to develop rational therapy, focused on disputing irrational beliefs.
moments.takeaway: Ellis prefigures Beck's cognitive turn by a decade.

moments.title: Reason and Emotion in Psychotherapy
moments.body: Ellis's book formalises the ABC model: Activating event, Beliefs, Consequences.
moments.takeaway: An accessible model spreads a therapeutic framework.

moments.title: Renamed REBT
moments.body: Ellis renames the approach Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy to include behavioural components.
moments.takeaway: Brand revisions track integration with parallel approaches.

now.title: Cognitive-behavioural lineage
now.body: REBT remains a recognised CBT variant. Its 'demandingness' and 'awfulising' constructs feed contemporary clinical formulation.
now.open_questions: How do REBT and Beckian CBT differ in measurable outcomes?

items.reflection: Ellis's confrontational style contrasted with Beck's collaborative tone; both shaped modern psychotherapy.

moments.title: Counselling and Psychotherapy
moments.body: Rogers proposes 'non-directive' therapy in which the therapist provides empathic understanding rather than interpretation.
moments.takeaway: Therapy can be reframed as client-led.

moments.title: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions
moments.body: Rogers specifies empathy, congruence and unconditional positive regard as necessary and sufficient for therapeutic change.
moments.takeaway: A bold empirical claim invited half a century of testing.

moments.title: A Way of Being
moments.body: Rogers extends person-centred principles to education, encounter groups and conflict resolution.
moments.takeaway: Therapeutic concepts can travel beyond clinical settings.

now.title: Common factors in therapy
now.body: Meta-analyses (Wampold) suggest much therapeutic outcome is explained by common factors close to Rogers's conditions.
now.open_questions: How should training balance technique-specific and common factors?

items.reflection: Rogers's humanistic psychology was once mainstream; CBT's rise has pushed it to the margins of evidence-based practice.

moments.title: Failure to escape traumatic shock
moments.who: Martin Seligman and Steven Maier, Pennsylvania
moments.body: Dogs exposed to unavoidable shock later fail to escape when escape becomes possible. Seligman names this learned helplessness.
moments.takeaway: Uncontrollable aversive experience produces a generalisable deficit.

moments.title: Helplessness model of depression
moments.body: Seligman proposes learned helplessness as a model of clinical depression, later reformulated with attributional style (Abramson et al., 1978).
moments.takeaway: Animal models contributed to cognitive theories of human disorder.

moments.title: Positive psychology launched
moments.body: Seligman uses his APA presidency to launch positive psychology, focused on flourishing and well-being.
moments.takeaway: Career arcs sometimes invert their own foundational findings.

now.title: Updated helplessness theory
now.body: Maier and Seligman's 2016 reformulation argues passivity is the default and control is learned, not helplessness.
now.open_questions: How does the neural basis of perceived control inform treatment of depression?

items.reflection: Seligman's trajectory mirrors a broader shift in clinical research priorities.

moments.title: On Being Sane in Insane Places
moments.body: Rosenhan's Science paper reports eight pseudopatients reporting one symptom each are admitted to psychiatric hospitals and have their behaviour reinterpreted as pathological.
moments.takeaway: Diagnostic context shapes the meaning attributed to behaviour.

moments.title: Spitzer reply
moments.body: Spitzer defends psychiatric diagnosis, arguing the pseudopatients' symptoms warranted admission.
moments.takeaway: Methodological debate continues long after a study's publication.

moments.title: Cahalan investigation
moments.body: Cahalan's investigation casts doubt on Rosenhan's records and identifies inconsistencies in his accounts.
moments.takeaway: Iconic studies sometimes do not survive archival scrutiny.

now.title: Diagnosis and stigma today
now.body: DSM-5 and ICD-11 are scrutinised for reliability and validity; the dimensional vs categorical debate continues.
now.open_questions: How should psychiatric classification handle culture-bound presentations and overlap between diagnoses?

items.reflection: Rosenhan's study became iconic for anti-psychiatry; its evidentiary basis is now contested.

moments.title: Compendium der Psychiatrie
moments.body: Kraepelin's textbook organises psychiatric disorders by clinical course and outcome rather than symptom snapshots.
moments.takeaway: Longitudinal observation reorganised psychiatric thinking.

moments.title: Dementia praecox vs manic-depressive insanity
moments.body: Kraepelin distinguishes a chronic deteriorating disorder (later schizophrenia) from a cyclical one (later bipolar).
moments.takeaway: Diagnostic categories are claims about underlying entities, not just labels.

moments.title: DSM-III neo-Kraepelinian turn
moments.body: DSM-III revives a Kraepelinian criteria-based approach after the analytic-dominated DSM-I and II.
moments.takeaway: Eras of psychiatric classification swing between description and theory.

now.title: RDoC and beyond
now.body: The Research Domain Criteria project (NIMH, 2009) attempts to ground psychiatric research in dimensions rather than DSM categories.
now.open_questions: Can biological dimensions outperform clinical categories for treatment selection?

items.reflection: Kraepelin's basic distinctions still organise psychiatric textbooks more than a century on.

moments.title: The Language and Thought of the Child
moments.body: Piaget's first major book observes children's spontaneous talk and reasoning in detail.
moments.takeaway: Naturalistic observation can ground a developmental theory.

moments.title: The Origins of Intelligence in Children
moments.body: Piaget's observations of his own three children ground his stage theory of cognitive development.
moments.takeaway: Foundational developmental theory began with very small samples.

moments.title: Children's Minds critique
moments.body: Donaldson shows many Piagetian tasks underestimate children when context is meaningful.
moments.takeaway: Task design shapes apparent developmental boundaries.

now.title: Piaget reconsidered
now.body: Strong stage theory is largely rejected, but Piagetian concepts remain core to developmental teaching.
now.open_questions: Which Piagetian constructs survive when tested with sensitive methods like looking-time?

items.reflection: Piaget's reach into education was profound, often via interpretations he would not have endorsed.

moments.title: Thinking and Speech, posthumous
moments.body: Vygotsky's major work appears the year of his death from tuberculosis, soon banned under Stalinism.
moments.takeaway: Political context can silence a theory for decades.

moments.title: First English translation
moments.body: Vygotsky's work reaches Western developmental psychology three decades after his death.
moments.takeaway: Re-discovery shapes which authors influence which generations.

moments.title: Mind in Society
moments.body: The edited Vygotsky reader introduces the zone of proximal development to English-speaking education.
moments.takeaway: Editorial choices shape canonical readings of foreign-language theorists.

now.title: Sociocultural theory in education
now.body: Scaffolding, dialogic teaching and culturally responsive pedagogy all draw on Vygotskyan thinking.
now.open_questions: How do digital tools change the social mediation of learning?

items.reflection: Vygotsky wrote in opposition to a purely individual psychology; his rehabilitation depended on political thaw.

moments.title: Bobo doll experiment
moments.body: Children who observe an adult hitting an inflatable doll later imitate the aggression, more so if the adult was rewarded.
moments.takeaway: Learning can occur through observation without direct reinforcement.

moments.title: Social Learning Theory
moments.body: Bandura formalises social learning theory, integrating attention, retention, motor reproduction and motivation.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical framework links observation to action.

moments.title: Social Cognitive Theory
moments.body: Bandura introduces reciprocal determinism and self-efficacy, broadening the model beyond imitation.
moments.takeaway: Agency re-enters social learning frameworks.

now.title: Self-efficacy and behaviour change
now.body: Self-efficacy is among the most cited constructs in education, health and organisational research.
now.open_questions: How do online influencers and short-form video alter classic observational-learning dynamics?

items.reflection: Bandura was Stanford's most cited psychologist; his death in 2021 closed an era.

moments.title: Illumination experiments begin
moments.body: Studies of lighting and productivity produce confusing results: productivity rises whether illumination is increased or decreased.
moments.takeaway: Confounds in field studies can yield more interesting findings than intended.

moments.title: Studies conclude
moments.body: The relay assembly studies become the basis for human relations management theory.
moments.takeaway: Industrial studies could reshape management as much as psychology.

moments.title: Re-analysis
moments.body: Re-analysis of the original Hawthorne data suggests effects were smaller and more time-dependent than the textbook account claims.
moments.takeaway: Foundational findings can shrink under scrutiny.

now.title: Observer effects in research
now.body: Modern research-design teaching cites Hawthorne effects in trials, ethnography and program evaluation.
now.open_questions: How should studies be designed to minimise or estimate observer effects?

items.reflection: The 'Hawthorne effect' is more rhetorical device than well-measured phenomenon.

moments.title: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
moments.body: Ioannidis's PLoS Medicine paper argues structural features of research produce a high false-positive rate.
moments.takeaway: Methodological argument can refocus a discipline on incentives.

moments.title: Reproducibility Project: Psychology
moments.body: A coordinated replication of 100 psychology studies reproduces effects at well below the original rate.
moments.takeaway: Coordinated replication produces evidence about a field as a whole.

moments.title: Many Analysts, One Dataset
moments.body: Twenty-nine teams analyse the same data and reach conflicting conclusions, highlighting analytic flexibility.
moments.takeaway: Researcher choices are themselves a source of variance.

now.title: Open science as norm
now.body: Preregistration, registered reports, open data and team science are standard at many journals.
now.open_questions: Will these reforms persist under publication-and-citation incentives?

items.reflection: Psychology became a leader, not a laggard, in research-reform debates.

moments.title: Dimensions of Personality
moments.body: Eysenck uses factor analysis on military-hospital data to identify extraversion and neuroticism as core dimensions.
moments.takeaway: Statistical methods structure personality theory.

moments.title: Crime and Personality
moments.body: Eysenck argues criminality reflects high extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism with under-aroused nervous systems.
moments.takeaway: Biological trait theory reaches into forensic psychology.

moments.title: Mass retractions
moments.body: An institutional inquiry recommends retraction of 26 Eysenck papers; 14 are retracted by 2020.
moments.takeaway: Posthumous reckoning can rewrite a research legacy.

now.title: Big Five and beyond
now.body: The Five-Factor Model dominates modern personality research; biological correlates are weaker than once claimed.
now.open_questions: What is the appropriate balance of personality and situational explanation for offending?

items.reflection: Eysenck's career illustrates both the power and the risks of bold trait theorising.

moments.title: REM sleep discovered
moments.who: Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman, Chicago
moments.body: Aserinsky records his eight-year-old son's eye movements during sleep and discovers regular rapid eye movement periods linked to dreaming.
moments.takeaway: Field-defining discoveries can come from quiet, low-cost observation.

moments.title: Sleep stages described
moments.body: Dement and Kleitman describe the now-canonical sleep stages and their cycling pattern.
moments.takeaway: A simple staging system makes sleep researchable.

moments.title: Activation-Synthesis hypothesis
moments.body: Hobson and McCarley propose dreams are the cortex's narrative response to brainstem activation.
moments.takeaway: A neurobiological account reframes a Freudian core topic.

now.title: Sleep, memory and health
now.body: Sleep is central to memory consolidation research, mental health and public health (insomnia, shift work, screens).
now.open_questions: How do dreaming and offline replay contribute to memory consolidation and creativity?

items.reflection: REM sleep is now a textbook concept; its discovery began as a curious father watching his son sleep.

moments.title: Stress concept introduced
moments.body: Selye's Nature letter describes a general adaptation syndrome in rats, with alarm, resistance and exhaustion stages.
moments.takeaway: A biological model of stress emerges from non-specific responses.

moments.title: The Stress of Life
moments.body: Selye's popular book brings stress into 20th-century medical and public vocabulary.
moments.takeaway: Scientific terms enter common language through trade writing.

moments.title: Cognitive appraisal
moments.body: Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model integrates appraisal and coping into stress theory.
moments.takeaway: Stress is psychological as well as physiological.

now.title: Allostatic load
now.body: Bruce McEwen's allostatic load concept integrates Selye and modern endocrinology, linking chronic stress to disease.
now.open_questions: How do early life stress and current stress interact in producing adult disease?

items.reflection: Selye introduced one of the most enduring metaphors in 20th-century medicine.

moments.title: Social Readjustment Rating Scale
moments.who: Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe, Washington
moments.body: Holmes and Rahe rank 43 life events by 'life change units', correlating their accumulation with illness.
moments.takeaway: Quantifying life events made stress epidemiologically tractable.

moments.title: Hassles and uplifts
moments.body: Daily hassles predict outcomes as well as major life events, challenging the major-events focus.
moments.takeaway: Everyday stressors matter as much as catastrophes.

moments.title: ACEs study
moments.who: Felitti and Anda, Kaiser and CDC
moments.body: The Adverse Childhood Experiences study links early-life stress to lifelong physical and mental health outcomes.
moments.takeaway: Cumulative early stress predicts adult disease.

now.title: Stress epidemiology
now.body: Stress measures are standard in health psychology, occupational health and life-course epidemiology.
now.open_questions: How should chronic societal stressors (poverty, discrimination) be measured alongside individual events?

items.reflection: Holmes and Rahe's checklist seems crude today but launched a generation of life-events research.

moments.title: Coming of Age in Samoa
moments.body: Mead's ethnography argues Samoan adolescence is largely free of the Sturm und Drang reported in the United States, supporting cultural over biological explanation.
moments.takeaway: Cross-cultural comparison was used to argue against universalist developmental claims.

moments.title: Freeman critique
moments.body: Freeman argues Mead was misled by informants and her conclusions overstated Samoan permissiveness.
moments.takeaway: Foundational ethnographies remain open to critical re-evaluation.

moments.title: Reanalysis and rebuttals
moments.body: Multiple commentators defend parts of Mead's work and contest Freeman, leaving a contested record.
moments.takeaway: Cross-cultural psychology lives with unresolved debates over its key cases.

now.title: Cross-cultural psychology
now.body: WEIRD sampling concerns (Henrich, 2010) renew interest in non-Western samples.
now.open_questions: How generalisable are psychological findings beyond WEIRD populations?

items.reflection: Mead's career sat at the boundary of anthropology and psychology.

moments.title: Independence and conformity
moments.body: Berry shows conformity varies between Inuit and Temne samples, linking subsistence ecology to social behaviour.
moments.takeaway: Cross-cultural psychology can locate variance in ecological context.

moments.title: Acculturation model
moments.body: Berry's two-dimensional model yields four acculturation strategies: integration, assimilation, separation, marginalisation.
moments.takeaway: Acculturation is a structured choice space, not a linear scale.

moments.title: International study of youth
moments.body: Their study of 7,000 immigrant youth across 13 countries finds integration most often associated with positive adaptation.
moments.takeaway: Large-scale studies can test acculturation theories empirically.

now.title: Migration psychology
now.body: Migration research uses acculturation frameworks in education, health and identity.
now.open_questions: How do digital diasporas and dual citizenship reshape acculturation dynamics?

items.reflection: Berry's framework remains the most cited single model in cross-cultural psychology.

moments.title: Still Face Paradigm
moments.body: Tronick's paradigm shows infants distressed and disengaged within seconds of a normally responsive caregiver becoming unresponsive.
moments.takeaway: Infants are active partners in social interaction from the first months.

moments.title: Online video
moments.body: A widely circulated video makes the still-face effect visually salient to a broader audience.
moments.takeaway: Public communication of paradigms shapes their reach.

moments.title: Mobile phone variants
moments.body: Parental phone use is shown to mimic some still-face effects on infant engagement.
moments.takeaway: Classic paradigms acquire contemporary relevance in unexpected ways.

now.title: Infant social cognition
now.body: The still-face paradigm is now standard in infancy research and clinical screening for maternal depression.
now.open_questions: How does screen-mediated caregiving affect infant social development?

items.reflection: A few seconds of laboratory footage helped reframe public understanding of infant emotional life.

moments.title: Subjective well-being review
moments.body: Diener's Psychological Bulletin review organises a scattered literature on happiness into a research field.
moments.takeaway: Review papers can found a subfield as much as primary research.

moments.title: Satisfaction With Life Scale
moments.body: The five-item SWLS becomes the most widely used measure of life satisfaction.
moments.takeaway: Short validated scales drive cumulative growth.

moments.title: Easterlin paradox revisited
moments.body: Whether national income predicts happiness above a threshold becomes a major economics-psychology debate.
moments.takeaway: Measurement choices shape policy conclusions.

now.title: Well-being measurement
now.body: ONS, OECD and the World Happiness Report use Diener-style measures. National well-being statistics inform policy.
now.open_questions: How should subjective well-being trade off against material indicators?

items.reflection: Diener's measurement work helped make 'happiness' a respectable variable in social science.

moments.title: 44 Juvenile Thieves
moments.who: John Bowlby, London Child Guidance Clinic
moments.body: Bowlby compares 44 thieves with 44 controls and reports prolonged maternal separation in many 'affectionless' cases.
moments.takeaway: Clinical comparison launched a maternal-deprivation hypothesis with policy ambitions.

moments.title: Maternal Care and Mental Health
moments.body: Bowlby's WHO report shapes post-war childcare policy across the Western world, despite a limited evidence base.
moments.takeaway: Policy can outrun evidence when a theory aligns with available institutions.

moments.title: Maternal Deprivation Reassessed
moments.body: Rutter distinguishes privation from deprivation and concludes Bowlby overgeneralised across different experiences.
moments.takeaway: Careful reassessment can rescue useful concepts from overclaims.

now.title: Early care and risk
now.body: Modern developmental research treats early relationships as one factor among many, with resilience possible after adversity.
now.open_questions: How do early relationships interact with later experience in shaping offending?

items.reflection: Bowlby's policy influence was enormous; his original evidentiary base was much thinner.

moments.title: The Process of Education
moments.body: Bruner's short book argues any subject can be taught honestly to any child at some level, introducing the spiral curriculum.
moments.takeaway: Cognitive psychology meets curriculum design at scale.

moments.title: Toward a Theory of Instruction
moments.body: Bruner identifies enactive, iconic and symbolic modes of representation as a developmental sequence.
moments.takeaway: Modes of representation give a tractable framework for instructional design.

moments.title: Scaffolding coined
moments.body: The term 'scaffolding' enters education in a paper on tutoring problem solving in children.
moments.takeaway: Terminological innovations can structure decades of practice.

now.title: Constructivism in classrooms
now.body: Bruner's ideas underpin inquiry-based learning, project-based learning and much primary curriculum design.
now.open_questions: How should scaffolding be calibrated when AI tutors interact with learners?

items.reflection: Bruner moved between cognitive psychology, anthropology and education through a long career.

moments.title: When Prophecy Fails
moments.body: A field study of a UFO cult after its prophesied apocalypse fails to occur shows believers redoubling commitment.
moments.takeaway: Cognitive dissonance can intensify, not abandon, belief.

moments.title: A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance
moments.body: Festinger formalises dissonance as psychological discomfort from inconsistency, motivating change in cognition or behaviour.
moments.takeaway: A single tight theory generated a large experimental literature.

moments.title: $1 vs $20 study
moments.body: Participants paid only $1 to lie about a boring task later rate it more enjoyable than those paid $20.
moments.takeaway: Counter-intuitive predictions strengthen a theory when confirmed.

now.title: Dissonance in polarised contexts
now.body: Dissonance research informs studies of political identity, conspiracy belief and behaviour-change interventions.
now.open_questions: How do online environments shape the resolution of dissonance through community signalling?

items.reflection: Festinger's dissonance theory remains a textbook example of psychology generating non-obvious predictions.

moments.title: The Psychology of Sex Differences
moments.who: Eleanor Maccoby and Carol Jacklin, Stanford
moments.body: Their review concludes most claimed sex differences are small or unsupported, with stronger evidence for aggression, verbal and spatial ability.
moments.takeaway: Reviewing a literature can puncture confident generalisations.

moments.title: The Two Sexes
moments.body: Maccoby emphasises sex-segregated play in childhood as a key context for gender development.
moments.takeaway: Context-level explanations complement individual-difference research.

moments.title: Gender similarities hypothesis
moments.body: Hyde's meta-meta-analysis finds most psychological gender differences are small or close to zero.
moments.takeaway: Cumulative evidence can shift a public narrative.

now.title: Gender beyond binary
now.body: Modern developmental psychology increasingly addresses gender identity diversity and intersectional analysis.
now.open_questions: How should classic sex-differences research be re-evaluated under broader conceptions of gender?

items.reflection: Maccoby spent decades insisting evidence about gender differences should be modest.

moments.title: Moral judgement of the child
moments.body: Kohlberg's doctoral thesis develops the moral judgement interview with hypothetical dilemmas, building on Piaget.
moments.takeaway: A doctoral framework can outlast its author.

moments.title: Six stages of moral development
moments.body: Kohlberg proposes six universal stages organised in three levels: preconventional, conventional and postconventional.
moments.takeaway: Stage theories carry strong universality claims.

moments.title: In a Different Voice
moments.body: Gilligan critiques Kohlberg for privileging justice reasoning over care reasoning and for under-sampling women.
moments.takeaway: Critical reframing can change the canon.

now.title: Moral psychology today
now.body: Haidt's moral foundations theory and dual-process accounts now dominate moral psychology, citing both Kohlberg and Gilligan.
now.open_questions: How universal are moral foundations across cultures?

items.reflection: Kohlberg's longitudinal samples were small and male-dominated; his framework still anchors discussion of moral reasoning.
